paragraphs.text: FEDERAL COURT
Court File No.: IMM-5590-25 (FICTIONAL)
BETWEEN:
KAVEH RAHIMI-LINDQVIST
Applicant
- and -
THE MINISTER OF CITIZENSHIP AND IMMIGRATION
Respondent
RESPONDENT’S MEMORANDUM OF ARGUMENT
(Prepared by counsel for the Minister, Department of Justice Canada – FICTIONAL)
PART I – OVERVIEW

1.	The Respondent, the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (the Minister), opposes the Applicant’s application for judicial review of the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) dated June 3, 2025. The RPD allowed the Minister’s application under section 108 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 (IRPA) and found that Mr. Kaveh Rahimi-Lindqvist had ceased to be a Convention refugee by reason of voluntarily re-availing himself of the protection of his country of nationality, under paragraph 108(1)(a).

2.	The RPD’s decision is reasonable. It is justified by the evidence of the Applicant’s three trips to his country of nationality on a national passport between 2021 and 2023, and its reasoning follows the elements of the test for re-availment.
PART II – FACTS

3.	The Applicant was recognized as a Convention refugee in 2017. He obtained a passport from the embassy of his country of nationality in 2020, which he renewed in 2022. He travelled to his country on that passport in November 2021, April 2022 and July 2023, each time for between two and four weeks. CBSA entry-exit records and the passport stamps confirm the dates.

4.	At the RPD hearing the Applicant testified that he returned to care for his ailing father, that he believed he would not be harmed because he stayed with relatives and did not leave the family home, and that he did not know that travelling on his passport could jeopardize his status. The RPD did not find that he lacked an intention to avail himself of protection, finding that the intention is presumed from the voluntary acts.
PART III – ISSUES
5.	The Respondent submits that the only issue is whether the RPD’s application of paragraph 108(1)(a) was reasonable.
PART IV – ARGUMENT
A. The standard is reasonableness

6.	The RPD’s decision is reviewed for reasonableness. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65 [Vavilov] at paras 10, 16 and 23–25. The Court does not reweigh the evidence or substitute its own view: Vavilov at para 125. The principle of deference to the specialized decision-maker in the field of immigration was affirmed in Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Khosa, 2009 SCC 12 at paras 59–67, and, before that, in Dunsmuir v New Brunswick, 2008 SCC 9 at paras 47–49, though the latter is now to be read as modified by Vavilov.
B. The RPD correctly applied the re-availment test

7.	Paragraph 108(1)(a) of IRPA provides that a claim for refugee protection shall be rejected, and a person is not a Convention refugee, if the person has voluntarily re-availed themself of the protection of their country of nationality. The test has three elements: voluntariness, intention and actual obtaining of protection. See Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Nilam, 2017 FC 153 at paras 25–27, and the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, Handbook and Guidelines on Procedures and Criteria for Determining Refugee Status, at paras 118–125.

8.	On voluntariness, the RPD found, as set out in the facts above at para 3, that the Applicant applied for and renewed the passport of his own accord. On intention, a person who applies for and uses a national passport is presumed to intend to avail themself of that country’s protection; the presumption is rebuttable. Ibid. The Applicant offered no evidence that rebuts it other than his lack of knowledge, which does not displace the presumption.

9.	On actual protection, the RPD relied on the Applicant’s trips: he was able to enter and leave his country without incident, and the RPD noted that it was the state’s passport that allowed him to do so. The RPD was entitled to conclude that this is actual obtaining of protection, as in Nilam at para 28.
C. The Applicant’s submissions invite reweighing

10.	The Applicant’s argument is that the RPD ought to have found that his motive, to see his father, outweighed the other facts. The RPD considered the evidence and explained why the humanitarian motive was not relevant to the question of intention: see the RPD’s reasons at paragraphs 22–25. A reviewing court should not interfere unless there are fundamental gaps or a lack of rationality (Vavilov at paras 100 and 105–106). No such flaw is present.

11.	To the extent the Applicant raises a new argument that the RPD should have applied subsection 108(2) of IRPA (the exception where the reasons for claiming refugee protection cease to exist) that argument was not raised before the RPD and should not be heard on judicial review: Alberta (Information and Privacy Commissioner) v Alberta Teachers’ Association, 2011 SCC 61 at paras 22–26.
PART V – ORDER SOUGHT

12.	The Respondent asks that the application for judicial review be dismissed, with no question for certification, and with costs only if the Court finds special reasons under rule 22 of the Federal Courts Citizenship, Immigration and Refugee Protection Rules, SOR/93-22.
